newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egyptian markets need new reforms - minister.
newsitem.headline: Egyptian markets need new reforms - minister.

text.p: In the next stage of economic reform the Egyptian government aims to tighten up regulations in capital markets and improve the way the judiciary handles commercial disputes, an economics minister said on Wednesday.

Youssef Boutros-Ghali, minister of state for economic affairs, told a conference on financial markets that such changes were needed to maintain the confidence of investors and indirectly to raise savings levels.
He said that the present savings level, at 18 percent of gross domestic product, was too low to generate the government's economic growth target of seven to nine percent a year.
"We need savings rates of 25 to 28 percent. Many will say you cannot raise savings rates that easily and they will be right. But it is a necessary condition.
"We can rely transitionally on foreign savings... but ultimately what will drive Egyptian growth rates is going to be Egyptian savings," he said.
In a presentation of the government's thinking on reform for the financial sector, he said:

"We need to improve the regulatory environment... The capital market needs a second generation of reform that addresses the behaviour of the participants and the behaviour of the government in these markets. It needs to be put in a code that does not affect market mechanisms but protects these markets from disturbances."
Officials say they are reviewing the current capital market law, passed in 1992 before the sudden explosion of stock market activity over the past year.

Asked about rumours of malpractices by Cairo brokers, especially that a grey market has developed in stocks for which the authorities have capped the price, Boutros-Ghali said the authorities were tackling the problem.
"All of these are teething pains. The system, the brokers, the clearing house are all in their infancy and these kinks are normal at this stage. I don't expect them to last long.
"These are fairly pedestrian concerns...but we are addressing it very seriously," he added.
The minister described the judiciary as the scourge of developing countries because of the time it took to enforce commmercial contracts in dispute.
"We need to develop contract enforcement mechanisms... the ability to settle disputes quickly, fairly and efficiently," he said. He did not mention specific proposals.
